cardPhrasings.note: Matched in CODE and never sent to the model. Trimmed, case-folded, trailing . and ! removed, then compared for EQUALITY. Measured: the model misrouted five of the eleven suggested phrasings in every trial while filling arguments perfectly, so the shapes with no ambiguity in them do not reach it.

parsed.becauseNotThis: The count and the noun disagree, so it is a sentence somebody typed carelessly rather than one of these shapes — and this tool renames pages the teacher's links point at. Guessing which half they meant is exactly what a fixed shape exists to avoid.
parsed.example: make room for two classes at Unit 3, Day 4

fills.howMany: <count>, as a number — words up to twelve are understood

parsed.notThis: make room for two class at Unit 3, Day 4
parsed.shape: make room for <count> class|classes at unit <unit>, day <day>

parsed.becauseNotThis: A comma means one PAGE was named, which has a title in it for the model to read out. Only a bare unit number is a whole unit.
As above: a comma names a page, not a unit.
No count, so there is nothing to fill `days` with and guessing one would create a number of pages nobody asked for.
parsed.example: add five more days to unit 4

fills.days: <count>, as a word up to twelve or a digit

parsed.becauseNotThis: The closing half is what makes the sentence unambiguous. Without it, 'duplicate' could mean several things and belongs with the model.
parsed.example: duplicate Unit 3, Day 2 as my next class

fills.duplicate: <page title>, with the capitals the teacher typed

parsed.shape: duplicate <page title> as my next class

parsed.becauseNotThis: A one-digit hour with no am or pm is morning or evening and nobody can tell which. A deploy set twelve hours wrong is a site that updates after the class it was meant for, so the doubt goes to the model rather than being resolved by a coin toss.

fills.when: <time> as HH:mm, with the day word in front of it when one was said — settled into a whole moment where the call is made, not here. Every accepted and refused spelling is in deployAtATime.

cardPhrasings.parsedNote: Families the matcher PARSES rather than compares, because the number or title in them is unbounded. They are matched in code for the same reason the literals are — the whole sentence IS the request, and reading an integer or a title off a fixed shape is not a judgement anybody needs a language model for. `notThis` is the near-miss each family must REFUSE, and it is the half that stops a family swallowing requests that belong to the model.

accepted.why: The shelf's own card, word for word (it offers it capitalised; matching is case-folded).
Written up against the digits, which is how a teacher in a hurry types it.

The same, already missing its last dot.
A whole hour with a meridiem needs no minutes to be exact.
The same, written up against the digit.
Noon, as a teacher writes it on a clock.

Midnight. Accepted for the same reason 'midnight' is: the approval card names the whole day and time before anything is set, so the reading is put in front of the teacher rather than guessed at silently.
The last minute of the day, and the one a teacher picks to mean 'tonight'.
24-hour time, and the form schedule_deploy's own schema asks for.
The same, in the afternoon.
Midnight in 24-hour time.
One of the two times a teacher writes with no digits in it.
The other. Treated exactly like '12 am' - one rule rather than two, and the card names the day it landed on.
The day word may lead.
…or follow. Either way it is carried as a word and settled where the call is made.
An explicit day word overrides the next-such-time rule, even into the past - see resolving.
The same, trailing.
'This section' is the only section a card can reach anyway; 'deploy this section now' is already a fixed phrasing, so the words are worth accepting here too.
'It' means the same thing as 'this section' and costs nothing to read.
Courtesy rather than content.
The same, at the other end.

A question mark is dropped INSIDE this family and not by the shared tidier - two fixed phrasings are matched by equality with a question mark in them ('what courses do i have?'), and a shared strip would stop those matching at all.

deployAtATime.note: The family 'deploy at <time>', matched in code and never sent to the model. AUTHORED, not generated: cardPhrasings.parsed carries one example and one near-miss, which is nowhere near enough to describe a family whose variable part is a TIME - one example would have the other platform build one spelling. The frame, after trimming, case-folding and removing a trailing . ! or ?: [please] deploy [it|this section] [today|tomorrow] at <time> [today|tomorrow] [please]. Anything else in the sentence - a section, a course, a weekday, a condition, a second request - falls through to the model. THE RULE THAT CARRIES THE MOST WEIGHT: a time with no am or pm must be written with two digits for the hour, because that is what 24-hour time looks like and it is the form schedule_deploy's own schema asks for. Measured on 2026-09-18: the smaller assistant sent 'Deploy at 6:30 AM' to deploy_section 10 trials out of 10, so a teacher who asked for half six tomorrow got a deploy to students on the spot (research/ai-assist/metal-routing-results.txt, issue #168). accepted and refused run the matcher; resolving runs the settling step that turns a bare time into a whole moment, and is pure input to output with an injected clock so it means the same thing in any time zone.

refused.why: A one-digit hour with no am or pm is morning or evening and nobody can tell which. A deploy set twelve hours wrong is a site that updates after the class it was meant for, so the doubt goes to the model - which is given the date in every message and is measured reading arguments out reliably.
A bare number is not a time anybody has spelled out. Read as an hour it would schedule a deploy off a number that might have been a unit or a section.
A dot is a sentence ending in this frame, not a clock separator.
A number, not a clock reading.
The hour and the meridiem disagree, so the sentence contradicts itself.
There is no such hour.
There is no such minute.
One digit of minutes is a slip, and it is not knowable whether 3 or 30 was meant.
Three digits of minutes is not a clock reading.
A one-digit hour with no meridiem, the same rule as 6:30. '00:30' is the spelling that says exactly what it means.
A teacher's idiom, and it means half past six in one country and half past five in another.
There is no time in the sentence at all.
No hour.

A section is named that this window cannot honour: the assistant window is scoped to ONE section and binds that section whatever the sentence said, so a card appearing to honour another section would answer a different question with total confidence.
A course is named, for the same reason.
A weekday is a day the frame does not read. It belongs to the model, which is given today's date in every message.
A day word on both sides is a sentence disagreeing with itself, and picking a half is what a fixed shape exists to avoid.
A question about ability as much as an instruction. 'Please' was measured as unambiguous courtesy and is accepted; this was not, so it goes to the model.
The opposite request. The frame requires 'deploy' as the first word for exactly this reason.

refused.input: deploy at 6:30 am if the preview looks ok
refused.why: A condition, which nothing here can evaluate.
A repeating schedule, which the tool cannot set.

refused.input: deploy at 6:30 am is too early
refused.why: Commentary about a time rather than a request to use it.
Publishing is not deploying, and the two are the distinction the assistant spends most of its words teaching.

resolving.why: Still to come today, so today is what it means.

The next such time, forwards, counting today while it is still to come - word for word the rule already applied to a bare weekday one unit up (schedule-rules.json, relativeDays). The guess is never silent: schedule_deploy waits for a button and its card names the whole moment, weekday and date included, before anything is written. The alternative considered and rejected was 'today at that time, always', which invents no rule but answers the shelf's own card with a refusal for most of the day.
The same minute is not still to come. Equal counts as gone, so nothing is ever scheduled for an instant that has already arrived.
Midnight and '12 am' are the same instant and are answered by the same rule; the card says which night it landed on.
An explicit day word is obeyed even when today would still have done.

Into the past ON PURPOSE. They named the day, so the app does not move it for them - and the existing refusal ('that has already passed') says so in the teacher's own words when they press the button.
Tomorrow crosses the end of the month, which is arithmetic on a calendar rather than on a number.

Already a whole moment - the form the model itself is told to send. Settling nothing is what makes the settler IDEMPOTENT, which is what lets the caller settle once, write its trail line from the settled arguments, and hand the same call straight on.

Not a clock reading this will complete. The matcher never produces it, and a MODEL that sends it still meets the tool's own 'I could not read that time' rather than having a day guessed onto a time nobody could read.
Unreadable, so it travels on exactly as it arrived and the teacher meets the runner's own refusal rather than a silent change of subject.

generated.note: These top-level keys are written by `Plantoir --write-contracts` from the app's own types and will be overwritten: cardPhrasings, tools, toolSchemas. Every other top-level key — nearMisses, scenarios, promptHistory, deployAtATime — is hand-written intent and is PRESERVED by a regeneration, so a case may be proposed from either platform. Listing them rather than naming two: the list was already two short when this was noticed, and a key nobody mentions is a key somebody deletes believing it was generated.

nearMisses.note: Must NOT match — each one only looks like a card phrasing, and answering the wrong question with total confidence is worse than routing it. The last three are the rollover's website question, and they record a KNOWN LIMIT rather than guarding a near-miss: the reply offers two sentences word for word, those exact strings are the only way back in, and a teacher who paraphrases matches nothing at all — re_date_classes is shown to no local model, so nothing catches the paraphrase and the section stays pinned to last year's website with nothing said. Both apps already pass these, so nothing goes red; they are written down so the limit is visible, and so a future looser matcher has to change this list on purpose. "publish next monday's class" is a different shape again: it is the near miss of a phrasing that DOES match, and it must reach the model precisely because "next Monday" is the one weekday word neither app will settle on its own - see schedule-rules.json, relativeDays.

cases.name: Up walks back, Down walks forward
the half-typed line is put aside, not thrown away
cases.why: Walking back Down past the newest entry hands the teacher's own half-written sentence back exactly as it was. Losing it is the thing that makes people stop trusting the arrow keys.

cases.name: Up at the oldest entry does nothing
cases.why: Rather than wrapping round to the newest, which reads as the keyboard having misfired.

cases.name: Down with no walk under way does nothing
the same thing twice in a row is remembered once
cases.why: Testing something by running it five times should not mean five presses of Up to get past it.

cases.name: an earlier, non-adjacent repeat is left alone
cases.why: The order a teacher did things in is the thing they are scrolling through. De-duplicating across the whole list would rewrite their history rather than shorten it.

cases.name: typing ends the walk
cases.why: Once a recalled line has been edited it is a new line, and Down must not silently replace what has just been typed.

cases.name: blank input is not remembered

keys.note: THE SAME ON BOTH PLATFORMS — decided 2026-08-16. Not a per-platform choice: a teacher who learns Up on one machine and finds it somewhere else on the other has learned nothing. Bind the arrow keys, in the composer, exactly as the mac does.

promptHistory.note: Walking back through what the teacher has asked before, the way a Terminal does. Modelled on a Terminal deliberately, because that is what teachers compare it to, and the details a Terminal gets right are the ones people notice only when they are missing. Steps are applied in order to a fresh history; `type` means the teacher edited the box, which ends the walk.

cases.when: the box holds more than one line
cases.why: The arrows have to move the caret between those lines. History would make a multi-line prompt impossible to edit.

cases.when: there is nowhere further to walk
cases.why: Up at the oldest entry, or Down with no walk under way. Passing the key on lets the field answer it — the caret moves to the start or end of the line, which is what the key means when history has nothing to offer.

passThroughWhen.note: The two cases where the arrows must do their ORDINARY job instead — the key event is passed on to the text field rather than swallowed. A key that silently does nothing reads as a dropped keystroke.

saying: roll this section over to a new year

cases.name: a rollover asks about the website and changes none of it
cases.why: The question has to reach the line a teacher READS. It was written into the reply's detail for a while, which the mac never surfaces for a write — so the feature was invisible in the app and worked over MCP alone, behind a green suite. Asserting it in the transcript is what makes that impossible to repeat. The second line matters as much: the re-dating has already happened by the time the question appears, so a teacher who does not answer must be told plainly that the website was NOT changed, or the feature quietly recreates the defect it was built to fix.

saying: roll this section over to a new year
roll this section over onto a new website

cases.name: answering the website question on a second turn still cuts the section loose
cases.why: The answer is the SECOND turn, and by then the pages are already on their dates — so the re-date plan changes nothing, and an early return on that made the whole answer a no-op: the reply talked about dates, never mentioned the website, and left the section pinned to last year's, behind an offer that looked like it had worked. Nothing exercised two turns in a row, which is why it survived. Both turns go through the plan card here, because asking before changing is ON unless a teacher turns it off.

expectTranscriptContains: teacher: roll this section over to a new year

saying: roll this section over to a new year
roll this section over to a new year

cases.name: a bare rollover asked a second time still asks about the website
cases.why: The mirror of the case above, and fixing that one left this one standing. That was the ANSWER turn returning early; this is the ASKING turn, one branch higher. A teacher who rolls over, ignores the question and comes back to ask again arrives with the dates already right — so the plan twin has nothing to propose, and returning "already on the day it should be" ended the turn there: asking before changing is ON by default and the surface returns early on anything that is not a plan, so the real call never ran and the teacher read nothing whatever about the website while the section stayed pinned to last year's site. With that setting turned OFF the same request was asked properly, which is what makes it a defect rather than a limitation: the question existed or not depending on a setting. The teacher line in the middle is load-bearing — it anchors the two sentences after it to the SECOND turn, and without it the first turn's reply satisfies them and the case cannot fail. `when` is "say" because the last turn is ANSWERED, not proposed: nothing is waiting to be agreed to, and a card there would offer a Go that changes nothing.

cases.name: deploy with a preview running
cases.why: The window's Deploy button stops any running preview first and waits for it to finish: stop mode finds a section's processes by working directory and would take the deploy's build with it.

cases.name: deploy with no preview running
cases.why: Nothing to stop. The reply says nothing about a preview either way — an assistant that accounts for what it had to do in order to obey is talking about itself.

cases.name: deploy with no section window open
cases.why: There is no button to press. This is the path Claude Code over MCP takes, and a deploy scheduled for half six in the morning. It must ask the same place for its launcher arguments as the button does, or a Cloudflare course goes to Netlify.

cases.name: deploy while that section is already busy
cases.why: A refusal in a whole sentence. The menu fragment that sits under a greyed-out menu item says nothing when read out in a conversation. Note the event: the assistant DOES press Deploy — the window is what declines, which is the real shape of it. This case was written expecting no event at all, and running it said otherwise.

cases.name: the deploy card is agreed to
cases.why: What the teacher chose is part of the history, in their own bubble. A conversation where the assistant asked, nothing answered, and something plainly happened is worse than one you cannot read back at all.

cases.name: the deploy card is cancelled
cases.why: The fact, and nothing else. Read which kind of card is pending BEFORE clearing it.

cases.name: a plan card is cancelled
cases.why: Here the reassurance IS the answer: the plan described changes to pages, so whether they happened is the part in doubt.

cases.name: a page edit, with a preview running
cases.why: The stop sits beside the WRITES, not beside the start: a preview left serving while the pages beneath it are rewritten serves a half-changed site, and the teacher's next refresh is a race they cannot see they are in. No expectReply on purpose — the reply is about the pages that changed, not about the preview; this case was written claiming the preview sentence, and running it said otherwise.

cases.name: a deploy asked for at a time is answered in code and asks about the MOMENT
cases.why: Measured on 2026-09-18: the smaller assistant sent this sentence to deploy_section 10 trials out of 10, so a teacher who asked for half six tomorrow got a deploy to students on the spot, behind an approval card that mentioned no time at all. Answered in code it cannot reach the model, and the card it does reach names the section, the destination and the whole moment. 'Section 1' is what is asserted because it is LOCALE-FREE and appears in the scheduled card on both platforms while appearing in the immediate one on neither: a formatted time is written '6:30 AM' here, '6:30 a.m.' on another Mac and with a different separator again in a 24-hour locale, so asserting one would pin the machine rather than the behaviour. The MOMENT is pinned instead by deployAtATime.resolving, which is pure and portable. Declined rather than approved because approving would write a real scheduled job.

scenarios.note: What must happen, and in what ORDER. The order is the assertion: every wrong ordering still passes a test that only checks all three events occurred. Event names are this contract's own; map them to whatever your app calls them. `given.saying` is a CONVERSATION — what the teacher types, in order, each turn settled before the next — because some behaviour exists only across turns; when it is absent a single turn is run, using whichever fixed phrasing reaches `given.pending`. `when` says what the teacher does on the LAST turn: "approve" presses Go on the card that is waiting (and fails if none is), "decline" presses Cancel, "say" means the last turn is ANSWERED rather than proposed, so nothing is waiting and a card there is the failure the case exists to catch; anything else is a tool name, called directly. `expectTranscriptContains` matches each named line by speaker PREFIX and sentence SUBSTRING, in order but not necessarily adjacent, and a line may satisfy more than one expectation — one reply often composes several named sentences into a single bubble. A literal line that is not a `wording.` name is matched as written, which is how a case anchors later expectations to a particular TURN.

tools.note: Three lists, deliberately. `all` is what the runner can execute; `local` is what the small model is SHOWN (the plan twins and remember_timetable are taken off, because the model never has to name a plan and dates it supplies are dates it may have invented); `mcpOnly` is the ten offered to Claude Code on top of everything — three asking for judgement about meaning, the rest either never needed by a model scoped to one section or already reachable by it through a fixed phrasing.
tools.planTwinsNote: A write with a twin is shown as a plan first. Four writes have none, deliberately: rebuild_preview changes no page, undo_last_change IS the remedy, deploy_section waits on its own button whatever plan mode says, and a cancelled scheduled deploy is remedied by scheduling it again.

absentHere.rejected: Adding it for symmetry. There is no boolean anywhere on this surface at all; the last was includeLinked, which asked the MODEL how far a publish or an unpublish should reach — the exact reasoning this design exists to keep out of a router. The rules live in AssistPublishPlanner instead, where they are written down once and tested.
absentHere.why: On Windows a batch of edits can be made with the preview suppressed and rebuilt once at the end. Here every change rebuilds, which is what the assistant's own system prompt promises a teacher, so there is nothing for the flag to mean.

departures.advertisedNotAccepted: The separator is what the SCHEMA tells the model, not the only character the runner accepts. AssistToolRunner is deliberately forgiving and splits on several — pages on semicolon or newline, codes and dates on comma, semicolon, newline and more. So a difference recorded here is a difference in what each side TELLS the model, which is worth knowing; it is not necessarily an incompatibility, and a suite should not assert one from it.
departures.howToReadThis: Each entry says a parameter is a string carrying a list, on which surfaces, and the separator this surface ADVERTISES to the model. It does NOT say what the other platform does — the mac cannot check that. A suite seeing both should intersect this list with its own schemas, and there are FOUR outcomes, not three: an ARRAY there is a real type departure; a string there with a DIFFERENT separator is a separator difference, worth asserting deliberately; a string there with the SAME separator is an agreement and nothing should be asserted about it; anything else is a real disagreement. Leaving the third case out turns a suite red for an agreement, which is how this note first read.
departures.note: How this surface's schemas differ from the Windows server's. Emitted so that side can READ them instead of keeping a hand-written copy — the copy is what made the two surfaces drift in the first place.
departures.notEnumeratedHere: Arguments the Windows server takes that this surface does not DECLARE. Mostly extra parameters on tools BOTH platforms serve — re_date_classes and read_remembered_timetable are the clearest, with the same name and different parameters on the two servers (GUI-IMPROVEMENTS.md row 447). Said precisely because the first version of this key said they were tools the mac does not serve at all, which is false: it serves both. The reason they stay in that platform's own list is that the mac does not declare those arguments, so it can neither test them nor notice when they change.

function.description: Make pages visible to students, along with every page they link to, then rebuild the section preview. The linked pages come by themselves — there is nothing to ask for and no way to leave them out, because a published page whose links lead nowhere is the one thing this must never make.
function.name: publish_pages

pages.description: The page titles to publish, separated by semicolons — for example "Unit 2, Day 3; Unit 2, Day 4". May be empty if you give dates instead.

function.description: TEACHERS SAY: "what happens if I take that down?", "check before you hide Unit 3, Day 2". Work out exactly what unpublishing pages from students would do, WITHOUT changing anything.
function.name: plan_unpublish_pages

before.description: Only classes strictly before this date. A date as YYYY-MM-DD, for example 2026-09-15. Leave empty for no limit.

course.description: The course code, for example ICS3U.

onOrAfter.description: Only classes on or after this date. A date as YYYY-MM-DD, for example 2026-09-15. Leave empty for no limit.

pages.description: The page titles to unpublish, separated by semicolons — for example "Unit 2, Day 3; Unit 2, Day 4". May be empty if you give dates instead.

function.description: TEACHERS SAY: "take Unit 4, Day 5 back down", "students shouldn't see it yet", "hide that page", "I posted it by mistake", "make it a draft again", "pull that lesson", "un-publish it". Unpublish pages, so students no longer see them, along with any page ONLY they link to; a page another class still links to stays put, and the result says which stayed and why.
function.name: unpublish_pages

before.description: Only classes strictly before this date. A date as YYYY-MM-DD, for example 2026-09-15. Leave empty for no limit.

course.description: The course code, for example ICS3U.

onOrAfter.description: Only classes on or after this date. A date as YYYY-MM-DD, for example 2026-09-15. Leave empty for no limit.

pages.description: The page titles to unpublish, separated by semicolons — for example "Unit 2, Day 3; Unit 2, Day 4". May be empty if you give dates instead.

function.description: TEACHERS SAY: "preview the site", "show me the preview", "start the preview", "open the preview", "rebuild the preview", "refresh what I'm looking at", "update the preview", "build it again". Build a section's preview and put it on screen, without changing any page.
function.name: rebuild_preview

course.description: The course code, for example ICS3U.

function.description: TEACHERS SAY: "undo that", "put it back", "that was wrong, revert it", "never mind, undo". Take back the most recent change this conversation made — the fix for publishing the wrong class in a hurry.
function.name: undo_last_change

function.description: TEACHERS SAY: "deploy the site", "put it online", "push it live", "send it to the website", "make it live for students", "upload the site". Put a section's website where students can actually reach it.
function.name: deploy_section

course.description: The course code, for example ICS3U.

function.description: TEACHERS SAY: "what happens if I schedule it for 6:30?", "check before you set that up". Work out what scheduling a deploy would mean, scheduling nothing.
function.name: plan_scheduled_deploy

classes.description: The class pages this deploy is meant to publish, separated by semicolons. Checked for whether they are published yet.

course.description: The course code, for example ICS3U.

when.description: When to deploy, as YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM in 24-hour time — for example "2026-09-09 06:30".

function.description: TEACHERS SAY: "deploy tomorrow's class at 6:30 AM", "put it live before school", "send it out at 7am", "schedule the deploy for Monday morning". Ask this computer to deploy a section at a set time.
function.name: schedule_deploy

course.description: The course code, for example ICS3U.

when.description: When to deploy, as YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM in 24-hour time — for example "2026-09-09 06:30".

function.description: TEACHERS SAY: "cancel that scheduled deploy", "don't send it in the morning after all", "call it off". Call off a deploy that was scheduled for a section.
function.name: cancel_scheduled_deploy

course.description: The course code, for example ICS3U.

function.description: TEACHERS SAY: "when does this class meet?", "what dates do you have for us?", "do you know our timetable?", "how many class days are left?". Read back the class dates recorded for a section, and where the teacher said they came from, changing nothing.
function.name: read_remembered_timetable

course.description: The course code, for example ICS3U.

function.description: Work out what recording these class dates would do, WITHOUT changing anything. Says how many days it would remember, the first and the last, and what it would replace.
function.name: plan_remember_timetable

course.description: The course code, for example ICS3U.

dates.description: Every day this class meets, as YYYY-MM-DD, separated by semicolons — for example "2026-09-08; 2026-09-10; 2026-09-14". Give the dates themselves; this tool does not open timetable files or work dates out from a pattern.

source.description: Where the dates came from, in the teacher's own words — for example "timetable.xlsx, block H" or "typed in by hand". Read back later, so a stale answer can be recognised. Leave empty if they did not say.

function.description: TEACHERS SAY: "here are the days we meet", "remember our timetable", "these are our class dates", "save these dates". Write down the days a section meets, so nothing has to ask for them again. Changes no page.
function.name: remember_timetable

course.description: The course code, for example ICS3U.

dates.description: Every day this class meets, as YYYY-MM-DD, separated by semicolons — for example "2026-09-08; 2026-09-10; 2026-09-14". Give the dates themselves; this tool does not open timetable files or work dates out from a pattern.

source.description: Where the dates came from, in the teacher's own words — for example "timetable.xlsx, block H" or "typed in by hand". Read back later, so a stale answer can be recognised. Leave empty if they did not say.

function.description: TEACHERS SAY: "what would the next class page be?", "which day comes next?", "show me before you add it". Work out which page adding the next class would create and which day it would fall on, WITHOUT changing anything.
function.name: plan_add_next_class

course.description: The course code, for example ICS3U.

function.description: TEACHERS SAY: "add an entry for the next class", "add tomorrow's class page", "start the next class", "add the next class", "make a page for our next class", "set up next day's lesson". Create the next class page in a section: it continues the unit the last class was in, and takes its date from the section's remembered timetable. Work out no numbers and no dates yourself — this tool does both. It starts unpublished, so students see nothing until the teacher publishes it.
function.name: add_next_class

course.description: The course code, for example ICS3U.

function.description: Work out what re-dating a whole section onto its recorded class dates would do, and change nothing. Shows every page that would move and why.
function.name: plan_re_date_classes

course.description: The course code, for example ICS3U.

function.description: TEACHERS SAY: "re-date my classes", "roll this section over to a new year", "put my classes on this year's dates". Re-date every class in a section onto the class dates on file, by POSITION — the first class takes the first date — and move the pages each class uses onto that class's day with it. Pages this section's Key Links points at move to the first day of class. Curriculum pages are left alone, because Plantoir dates those itself on every build. Set `website` when the teacher is rolling a section over to a NEW YEAR and has said which website they want: "new" starts a fresh one, so publishing no longer replaces last year's site, and "same" keeps last year's address. Ask them first — never choose for them, and leave it out for an ordinary re-dating.
function.name: re_date_classes

course.description: The course code, for example ICS3U.

website.description: Either "new" or "same", when a teacher rolling this section over to a new year has said which website they want. LEAVE THE KEY OUT otherwise — any other text counts as a rollover and asks the teacher which website they want, which an ordinary re-dating must never do.

function.description: TEACHERS SAY: "what courses do I have?", "list my courses". List the courses in this working folder: the code, the name, which sections each one has, and where each publishes to. Call this first when a teacher mentions a course and you are not certain of its exact code — guessing a code reaches the wrong course silently.
function.name: list_courses

function.description: Work out what adding several class pages to a unit would do, and change nothing. Shows what each page would be called and the day it would land on. Call this first and show the teacher what it said.
function.name: plan_add_classes

course.description: The course code, for example ICS3U.

howMany.description: How many class pages to add to that unit.

unit.description: The unit number to add days to, for example 4.

function.description:
TEACHERS SAY: "add five more days to Unit 4". Add several class pages to a unit, dated to the days this section actually meets, continuing from the last day that unit already has. Call plan_add_classes first and show the teacher what it said.

The pages arrive UNPUBLISHED — empty skeletons for the teacher to write, which stay out of the site until they publish them. An existing page is never written over, the course is backed up first, and undo_last_change takes back what this created.
function.name: add_classes

course.description: The course code, for example ICS3U.

howMany.description: How many class pages to add to that unit.

unit.description: The unit number to add days to, for example 4.

function.description: Work out what making room part-way through a unit would do, and change nothing. Names every page that would be renamed, every class that would move to a later day, and every link that would be rewritten. Call this first and show the teacher what it said, in full — this moves more pages than anything else here.
function.name: plan_make_room_for_classes

atDay.description: The day number the new class takes. That day and every later day in the unit are renumbered to make room.

course.description: The course code, for example ICS3U.

howMany.description: How many classes to make room for. Leave empty for one.

unit.description: The unit number to add days to, for example 4.

function.description:
TEACHERS SAY: "make room for a class at Unit 3, Day 4". Insert one or more classes part-way through a unit: the later days of that unit are renumbered, every link that pointed at them is rewritten, the classes that follow move onto later class days, and the new pages arrive unpublished.

Call plan_make_room_for_classes FIRST and show the teacher what it said. The course is backed up first. Once other classes have moved, "undo that" can no longer take this back and the backup is the way out — so tell the teacher to look the section over in Plantoir before publishing anything.
function.name: make_room_for_classes

atDay.description: The day number the new class takes. That day and every later day in the unit are renumbered to make room.

course.description: The course code, for example ICS3U.

howMany.description: How many classes to make room for. Leave empty for one.

unit.description: The unit number to add days to, for example 4.

function.description: Call this FIRST, before doing anything else with a section. It returns a short explanation of what publishing and deploying mean in Plantoir — say it to the teacher word for word. It answers once per section: after that it says so, and you should get straight on with what was asked rather than repeating it.
function.name: explain_publishing

course.description: The course code, for example ICS3U.

function.description: Make a full copy of one course, which the teacher can restore from inside Plantoir. Do this before any bulk editing of a course's files — INCLUDING edits you make directly rather than through these tools, which nothing else backs up. Course folders are not in version control, so a copy is the only way back.
function.name: back_up_course

course.description: The course code, for example ICS3U.

function.description: List this course's curriculum expectations with their FULL WORDING, changing nothing. Call this when a teacher asks you to point a page at the expectations it covers. Read the page first, then read these, then decide which genuinely fit — that judgement is yours to make and the tools cannot make it. Propose the codes to the teacher with your reasons and let them choose; do not add expectations they have not agreed to.
function.name: list_curriculum_expectations

course.description: The course code, for example ICS3U.

matching.description: Only list expectations whose code or wording contains this. Leave empty for all.

function.description: Work out what adding curriculum transclusions to a page would do, changing nothing. Show the teacher what it says — it quotes each expectation's wording so they can tell whether it fits their lesson without looking it up — then wait for them to agree.
function.name: plan_curriculum_mentions

codes.description: The expectation codes to add, separated by commas — for example "A1.1, A2.2".

course.description: The course code, for example ICS3U.

page.description: The page title, for example "Movement Concepts".

function.description: Add transclusions of curriculum expectations to a page, inside the curriculum markers so a course installed without curriculum still builds. Call plan_curriculum_mentions FIRST and get the teacher's agreement to the specific codes. Changes nothing else on the page, and changes no page's visibility. The course is backed up first.
function.name: add_curriculum_mentions

codes.description: The expectation codes to add, separated by commas — for example "A1.1, A2.2".

course.description: The course code, for example ICS3U.

page.description: The page title, for example "Movement Concepts".

toolSchemas.note: The tool definitions exactly as each client sends them. The DESCRIPTIONS are measured, not decorative — see the note on steering with code rather than with tool descriptions. `local` is what the on-device model is shown; `mcp` is what Claude Code sees. Point a routing measurement at these rather than at a copy.
